body:
Not all Gujarat ports followed Surat's experience

Although Surat's earlier maritime dominance declined, Gujarat's coastline continued to support trade through several ports. Khambhat and Bharuch were longstanding commercial centres. In Saurashtra, the princely state of Bhavnagar developed maritime commerce through Bhavnagar port and other centres, including Ghogha and Mahuva.

These ports did not necessarily handle identical goods or enjoy equal commercial success. Their importance depended on navigational conditions, connections with inland producers, shipping arrangements and the policies of the authorities controlling them.

Bhavnagar as an example of princely-state initiative

Bhavnagar remained a princely state under British supremacy rather than becoming an ordinary district of the Bombay Presidency. Its rulers and administrators pursued commercial and transport improvements within the limits of that relationship.

The state invested in port-related development and railway construction. According to Western Railway's historical account, the railway line from Bhavnagar Terminus to Wadhwan City was inaugurated in December 1880. The project was undertaken using the state's own resources.

This demonstrates an important distinction: railways in colonial Gujarat were not all constructed by one British railway company. Some princely governments financed or supported their own railway systems.

Comparing different administrative settings

SettingPolitical arrangementEconomic significance
Directly administered Bombay Presidency districtsBritish officials administered revenue and public worksIntegration into colonial ports, railways and commercial markets
Baroda StateGaekwad ruler under British political supremacyState policies and railway initiatives alongside wider colonial transport links
Bhavnagar StatePrincely administration under British supremacyMaritime trade, port improvement and a state-funded railway
Smaller eastern princely territoriesLocal chiefs with varying powers under political supervisionRevenue disputes, forest access and contested local authority

The table shows why a single statement about British land or railway policy cannot automatically be applied to every territory. Local arrangements mattered.

The importance of political agencies

In eastern Gujarat, the British used political agents to supervise relations with princely rulers and chiefs. The Rewa Kantha Political Agency became an important institution for this purpose during the 19th century.

The Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency records the appointment of a political agent for Rewa Kantha in 1826. Its account describes disputes involving chiefs, tribute, jurisdiction and revenue. Such conflicts formed part of the setting in which resistance developed around Jambughoda and neighbouring territories.

Prelims focus

  • Bhavnagar was a princely state with important maritime trade.
  • Bhavnagar, Ghogha and Mahuva were associated with the state's port economy.
  • Bhavnagar-Wadhwan City railway service was inaugurated in December 1880.
  • BB&CI Railway and princely-state railway initiatives should be distinguished.
  • Rewa Kantha Political Agency was important in supervising eastern Gujarat's princely territories.
  • Trap: Indirect British influence over a princely state did not make that state identical to a directly administered British district.

[Government of Gujarat, Bhavnagar District Administration, History of Bhavnagar, sections on maritime trade and railways, consulted 20 November 2026; Government of India, Western Railway, History of Bhavnagar Division, pp. 1-2, consulted 20 November 2026; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. VI, Rewa Kantha, ch. VII, pp. 61-66, 1880, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Company-linked BB&CI and state-funded Bhavnagar railways followed different paths while supporting links between inland centres, markets and ports.
pictures.caption: Colonial Gujarat contained both company-linked and princely-state transport initiatives.

title: Ports and Princely States: Different Paths of Economic Development

body:
Land revenue and the cultivator

Agriculture remained the principal livelihood of a large proportion of Gujarat's population during the colonial period. The government expected agricultural land to provide revenue, while cultivators depended on harvests for food, seed, rent, taxes and repayment of loans.

In much of the directly administered Bombay Presidency, the British developed the ryotwari revenue system. Under this arrangement, revenue assessment was made with individual cultivators, or ryots, rather than through a permanently recognised class of zamindars. Assessments could be revised through later settlements.

This differed from the Permanent Settlement of 1793, associated principally with Bengal, where the government's demand from recognised zamindars was fixed permanently. Gujarat must not be described as uniformly governed by Bengal's Permanent Settlement. Moreover, princely-state revenue systems could differ from those used in British districts.

Commercialisation of agriculture

Commercialisation of agriculture means producing crops increasingly for sale in markets rather than primarily for household consumption. Cotton was an important commercial crop in western India.

British textile mills needed raw cotton. International demand therefore influenced what farmers cultivated, the prices they received and the credit offered by merchants. Commercial cultivation could provide additional earnings when prices were favourable, but it also exposed farmers to fluctuations in distant markets.

The American Civil War and the cotton boom

The American Civil War, 1861-1865, disrupted cotton supplies from the United States to Britain. British manufacturers searched for alternative sources, including India.

Demand for Indian raw cotton increased sharply. Traders and moneylenders extended advances to secure supplies, encouraging cultivators in western India to expand cotton production. However, the increased demand did not guarantee permanent prosperity.

After the war, American cotton exports recovered and the extraordinary demand for Indian cotton weakened. Falling prices and the withdrawal of credit created problems for cultivators who had borrowed in anticipation of continued high earnings. The extent of these effects varied by locality and by a farmer's access to land, credit and markets.

Why rural indebtedness increased

A farmer who needed cash to pay revenue or meet household expenses might borrow from a moneylender. If the crop failed, cotton prices declined or repayment became due before a profitable sale, the farmer could find it difficult to clear the debt. Additional borrowing could then increase dependence on creditors.

Railways and ports helped agricultural goods reach markets, but faster transport alone did not eliminate these risks. The same commercial network that opened opportunities for traders and some cultivators could make poorer households more vulnerable to price changes.

Connecting agrarian pressure with the eastern belt

Commercial cotton cultivation was particularly important in the agricultural districts of western India. In Gujarat's eastern hills, a different but related set of problems involved access to forest land, the authority of local chiefs, cultivation assessments and revenue collection. These pressures helped create the conditions for tribal resistance.

Prelims focus

  • Ryotwari settlements dealt with individual cultivators and were important in the Bombay Presidency.
  • Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal in 1793; it was not the uniform land system of Gujarat.
  • Commercialisation of agriculture increased production for markets.
  • American Civil War: 1861-1865.
  • The war increased British demand for Indian cotton; the recovery of American supplies later reduced the exceptional demand.
  • Trap: An increase in cotton exports did not necessarily mean that every cotton cultivator became wealthier.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, ch. 3, Ruling the Countryside, pp. 28-31; NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class 11, ch. 2, Colonial Rule and Crafts, pp. 22-25; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, ch. 1, Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence, pp. 5-9.]

pictures.alt: Civil War disruption boosted Indian cotton demand, advances and cultivation; recovering American exports weakened prices and made some debts hard to repay.
pictures.caption: A temporary overseas cotton boom could be followed by falling prices and greater debt.

title: Agrarian Change: Land Revenue, Commercial Cotton and Rural Debt

body:
The eastern tribal belt

The forested and hilly regions of eastern Gujarat formed part of a larger tribal belt extending into neighbouring Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra. Within present-day Gujarat, areas such as Panchmahals, Dahod, Jambughoda, Chhota Udepur, Rajpipla and the Dangs are important when studying the history of tribal communities and colonial rule.

Bhils were present across several parts of this wider region. Naikdas, also written as Nayakdas or Nayakas in different accounts, were particularly significant in resistance movements around Panchmahals and Jambughoda.

Bhil and Naikda are not interchangeable names. They identify different community groupings, although their histories intersected in the eastern Gujarat region. The word Naik could also function as a title for a local leader; it does not, by itself, prove that the person belonged to the Naikda community.

Livelihoods depended on land and forest access

Tribal households did not all practise one occupation. Their livelihoods could include settled farming, shifting cultivation, grazing, gathering forest produce, hunting, local trade and wage labour.

In shifting cultivation, a patch of vegetation was cleared for cultivation, crops were grown for a period, and the plot was later left fallow while cultivation moved elsewhere. NCERT records the practice among Bhil cultivators in Gujarat.

Forests also supplied food, fuel, fodder, timber for household needs and products that could be exchanged or sold. Access to these resources was therefore an economic necessity, not merely a customary preference.

Political authority before and during colonial expansion

In several regions, tribal chiefs and headmen exercised local authority or held customary claims to dues, land and resources. Their arrangements with neighbouring rulers varied. Some were involved in protecting routes, supervising local affairs or receiving customary payments.

As British influence expanded, colonial authorities sought more regular taxation, clearer territorial control and stronger policing. Political agents intervened in disputes among rulers and chiefs. Local communities could lose customary authority or face pressure to adopt forms of settled cultivation preferred by officials.

Forest rules and revenue demands

During the 19th century, colonial forest policies increasingly restricted activities such as cutting timber, grazing, hunting and shifting cultivation. The Indian Forest Act of 1865 strengthened the legal basis for state control over forests. The 1878 forest legislation distinguished reserved, protected and village forests. In reserved forests, customary access could be severely restricted.

Railway construction increased demand for timber, including wooden railway sleepers. The colonial government's interest in commercial forestry could therefore conflict with the everyday needs of forest-dependent communities.

These measures were introduced at different times. They help explain the broader development of colonial control, but they cannot all be treated as causes of every earlier uprising.

Chronology matters: a revolt in 1838 cannot have been caused by the Forest Act of 1878. Earlier conflicts involved changing political authority, tribute, revenue demands and interference with established local practices; later forest legislation intensified restrictions.

Prelims focus

  • Bhils inhabited a wider belt crossing the boundaries of present-day Gujarat.
  • Naikda resistance was especially important around Panchmahals and Jambughoda.
  • Tribal livelihoods could combine cultivation, forest produce, grazing and labour.
  • Indian Forest Act: 1865; major forest classification legislation: 1878.
  • Reserved forests were subject to particularly strong restrictions on customary use.
  • Trap: Do not confuse a community name with the leadership title Naik, or use a later forest law to explain an earlier revolt.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, ch. 4, Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age, pp. 39-47, especially pp. 43-46; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-I, Class 9, ch. 4, Forest Society and Colonialism, pp. 78-87; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. VI, Narukot, sections History and Land, pp. 174-176, 1880, consulted 20 November 2026; Alf Gunvald Nilsen, Subalterns and the State in the Longue Duree, Journal of Contemporary Asia, section on Bhil resistance, 2015, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Rural households tend a small field and carry forest produce beside thatched homes and wooded hills in 19th-century eastern Gujarat.
pictures.caption: In eastern Gujarat, cultivation and access to forest resources supported many rural households.

pictures.alt: Revenue, political, policing and forest controls converge on tribal livelihoods, reducing access and creating disputes and pressure for change.
pictures.caption: Colonial revenue and forest administration altered access to resources used by tribal communities.

title: Bhil and Naikda Communities: Livelihoods and Pressures in Eastern Gujarat

body:
Why the eastern region witnessed repeated conflict

The territories around Jambughoda, Baria, Chhota Udepur and Godhra were politically complex. Local chiefs, the Gaekwad government, neighbouring rulers and British political agents made overlapping claims to authority and revenue.

When officials sought to collect dues, enforce political settlements or strengthen policing, local communities could regard these actions as an interference with established rights and livelihoods. Resistance did not always take the form of one continuous rebellion; it occurred in separate episodes under different leaders.

Local unrest in 1837 and the wider rising of 1838

A contemporary account of Narukot, associated with the Jambughoda area, describes opposition to harsh revenue collection by a Gaekwad-controlled post in 1837. The resulting conflict was followed by wider disturbances involving Naikda groups.

The 1838 Naikda rising affected areas including Baria, Chhota Udepur, Jambughoda and Godhra. The Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency identifies several leaders or leading participants, including Keval of Baras, Jalam Rupa Naik and Viram Naik.

British officers organised a military response. Captain James Outram prepared a campaign plan, and troops under Major Forbes were sent into the affected areas in February 1838. British forces received assistance from neighbouring rulers, including the chiefs of Baria and Chhota Udepur.

The rising was suppressed during 1838. Some participants were imprisoned, while others surrendered under conditions imposed by the authorities. The episode demonstrates that British political intervention and princely-state interests could combine against local resistance.

The later rising connected with 1857

The wider Indian uprising that began in 1857 also affected the political situation around eastern Gujarat. In this region, an important phase of Naikda resistance took place in 1858 and continued into 1859.

The Gazetteer names Keval Dama and Rupa Gobar as leaders of the 1858 rising, which was concentrated mainly in the Panchmahals area. Armed groups were active around Jambughoda and neighbouring territories. Colonial accounts also record movements of forces associated with Tatya Tope through the wider region during late 1858.

The fighting continued into 1859 before colonial and allied forces restored control. According to the Gazetteer, Keval Dama surrendered in March 1859 and Rupa Gobar in May 1859.

Distinguishing the 2 episodes

The 1838 rising belonged to the earlier period of contested political supervision, tribute and local authority. The 1858-1859 rising took place in the context of the wider rebellion of 1857, although it also reflected regional grievances.

The events should not be treated as identical simply because they involved Naikda resistance and overlapping locations. Another major rising followed in 1868, under Rup Singh Naik and Joria Bhagat.

Prelims focus

  • 1838: an important Naikda uprising in eastern Gujarat.
  • Important locations included Baria, Chhota Udepur, Jambughoda and Godhra.
  • Keval of Baras, Jalam Rupa Naik and Viram Naik appear in accounts of the 1838 rising.
  • Outram planned and Major Forbes commanded the British military response in 1838.
  • Keval Dama and Rupa Gobar were associated with the 1858-1859 resistance.
  • Trap: The uprising beginning nationally in 1857 should not make every eastern Gujarat resistance episode a single event dated only to 1857.

[Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. VI, Rewa Kantha, ch. VII, History, pp. 62-64, and Narukot, History, pp. 174-175, 1880, consulted 20 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Panchmahal History, section on the events of 1858, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Separate timelines distinguish the 1837–1838 Naikda unrest and rising from the 1858–1859 resistance, with their leaders and outcomes.
pictures.caption: Naikda resistance developed through distinct episodes rather than a single uninterrupted revolt.

title: The Naikda Uprising of 1838 and Resistance During 1857-1859
